Chapter 06

06

Understanding design foundations

Before buttons and menus, there's a smaller set of decisions that everything else inherits: colours, text, spacing and layout. They're the cheapest part of a design system to set up, and the most expensive part to get wrong.

Read this if

You're about to decide your product's colours, type or spacing, or you want to understand how a design decision turns into code without anyone retyping it.

What you'll leave with
  1. What counts as a "foundation", and what doesn't.
  2. Why changing a foundation is a big deal, explained through a simple idea called blast radius.
  3. How a decision travels from a designer's head into the product's code.

In this chapter

  1. 06.1What foundations are
  2. 06.2Why foundations matter: blast radius
  3. 06.3From a designer's decision to the product's code

06.1What foundations are

Think of building a house. Before anyone chooses kitchen cabinets, someone has decided the ceiling height, the size of a standard door and where the plumbing runs. Every room inherits those decisions. Get them right and everything fits. Get them wrong and every room fights the house.

Foundations are the same thing for a digital product. They're the basic visual decisions that every button, card and page inherits. They aren't components themselves, but every component is built out of them. Different design systems give them slightly different names (IBM's Carbon calls them "elements"; Google's Material calls them "styles" and "foundations"), but the list is remarkably consistent.3031

Chapter 07

Colour

Which colours you use, for what, and how they work in dark mode.

Chapter 08

Typography

Fonts, text sizes, and how headings and body text relate.

Chapter 09

Spacing

How much room goes between and inside things.

Chapter 10

Layout

Grids, screen sizes and how pages are arranged.

Also

Elevation

Shadows, and what sits on top of what.

Also

Shape

How rounded corners are, and how thick borders are.

Also

Motion

How long animations take and how they move.

Also

Icons

Sizes, line thickness and style.

This edition covers the four with the biggest effect on how good your product feels: colour, typography, spacing and layout. The others follow exactly the same thinking.

06.2Why foundations matter: blast radius

Here's a useful way to think about any design decision: how many places does it affect? We call that its blast radius. Changing the label on one button affects one button. Changing the colour used for all secondary text affects every screen in every product. Foundations have the biggest blast radius of anything in a design system.

That double edge is the whole point. A wide blast radius is what makes foundations powerful: fix a contrast problem once and it's fixed everywhere. It's also what makes them risky: pick a text size that's slightly too small and every screen inherits it. Four things in particular are decided at this level:

QualityWhether text is readable and whether headings stand out from body text is decided here. Muddy text sizes make every screen muddy.
ConsistencyOffering twelve spacing values instead of "whatever looks right" makes consistency the default instead of something checked in review.
FlexibilityNaming colours by their job (07.4) is what later makes dark mode and new brands possible without touching any components.
SpeedFewer choices mean faster decisions. "Which of these twelve?" is a much quicker question than "how many pixels?"

06.3From a designer's decision to the product's code

Here's the problem foundations have to solve. A designer decides the primary button should be a particular shade of orange. In a traditional handover, she writes #AB2800 on a spec. An engineer copies it into the code. Another engineer, on another team, copies it from a screenshot and gets #AA2900. A year later, nobody knows which is right, and changing it means finding every copy.

Design tokens fix this by making sure a decision is written down once and everything else reads from that one place. The steps look like this:

Notice that there are two names in the middle. The first, brand-700, describes the colour itself: it's the 700 shade of our brand orange. The second, action-primary, describes its job: it's the colour for main actions. Buttons use the job name, not the colour name. That small extra step is what makes dark mode possible later. In dark mode, "the colour for main actions" can point to a lighter orange, and no button needs to change. Chapter 07 explains this properly.

A shared format for tokens

For years, every design tool and code library stored tokens in its own format, which made moving between them painful. In October 2025 the W3C Design Tokens Community Group, an industry group that includes people from Adobe, Google, Microsoft and others, published the first stable version of a shared format.432 Documented It's a simple structured text file. Each token has a type (colour, size and so on) and a value, and tokens can point to each other using curly brackets, like {color.brand.700}. (Strictly speaking it's a community group report rather than an official W3C standard, but it's the format most token tools are now converging on.)

Here's what a small piece of Ledgerly's tokens looks like in that format. You don't need to be able to read code to get the idea: raw colours at the top, job names that point to them in the middle, and a button that points to a job name at the bottom.

Practice Tokens first, components second

This is Rule #4 of how we work, and the most important sequencing decision in a design system. Components built before tokens exist end up with colour codes and sizes typed directly into them, which someone has to find and replace later. Tokens set up first make every component ready for themes and changes from day one.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Foundations are the basic visual decisions everything else inherits: colour, type, spacing and layout, plus a few more.
  2. They have the biggest blast radius in the system, so they deserve the most careful thought.
  3. Tokens let a decision be written once and read everywhere: by design tools and by the code for every platform.
  4. Name the raw value, then name its job. Components use the job names.

Chapter 07

07

Colour systems

Colour is the foundation teams get wrong most often, and the one where getting it right pays off fastest. We'll go step by step, from how colours are described, to building a palette, to making dark mode a simple switch. Every value in this chapter is calculated, not guessed.

Read this if

You're creating or fixing a colour palette, planning dark mode or a second brand, or your accessibility audits keep flagging text that's hard to read.

What you'll leave with
  1. Why the way you describe colour matters, and why we recommend a model called OKLCH.
  2. A repeatable method for building a palette, with a complete worked example.
  3. A way of naming colours that makes dark mode and new brands a settings change.

In this chapter

  1. 07.1Why colour goes wrong
  2. 07.2How colour is described
  3. 07.3Building a palette, step by step
  4. 07.4Making sure people can read it
  5. 07.5Naming colours by their job
  6. 07.6Colours that respond: hover, press and focus
  7. 07.7Dark mode, brands and white-labelling
  8. 07.8Questions teams always ask about colour

07.1Why colour goes wrong

Let's start with a story we've seen in some form at almost every company we've audited.

Scenario340 greys and no way to switch them
The situation

A five-year-old product finally commits to dark mode. An engineer searches the code for colour values to see how big the job is.

What they find

340 different colour values, most of them greys that are almost, but not quite, the same. Some are for text, some for borders, some for backgrounds. Nothing in the code says which is which.

Why it matters

To build dark mode, someone has to look at every one of those 340 values in context and decide what it should become. A two-sprint feature turns into a two-quarter project.

Nobody set out to create 340 greys. A designer picked a grey that looked right for a divider. Another picked a slightly lighter one for a caption. An engineer approximated one from a screenshot. Each choice was reasonable. Together they're unmanageable.

There's a second, quieter problem too: text that's hard to read. Pale grey text looks elegant in a design file on a bright monitor. On a laptop in sunlight, or for someone with less-than-perfect eyesight, it disappears. WebAIM's 2025 scan of the world's top million home pages found text with too little contrast on 79.1% of them, making it the single most common accessibility problem on the web.10 Documented

A colour system solves both problems. It gives you a small, deliberate set of colours, each checked for readability, each named by the job it does. The rest of this chapter shows you how to build one.

07.2How colour is described

To a computer, a colour is just numbers, and there are several ways of writing those numbers down. They're called colour models. You've probably seen some of them: #CC3C00 or rgb(204, 60, 0). The model you use matters more than you'd think, because it decides which questions are easy to answer. For a design system, the most important question is: is this colour lighter or darker than that one, and by how much? Readability, hierarchy and hover effects all depend on it.

ModelDescribes colour asGood forThe catch
RGB / HEXAmounts of red, green and blue lightHow screens actually work; every tool understands itUnreadable to humans. Nobody can look at #CC3C00 and know how to make it 10% lighter.
HSL / HSVHue (which colour), saturation, lightnessPicking colours by feel; most colour pickers use itIts "lightness" isn't what your eyes see. A yellow and a blue with the same HSL lightness look completely different.
OKLCHLightness (0 to 1), chroma (how colourful), hue (which colour)Building palettes and themesSome combinations can't be shown on normal screens, and its lightness isn't exactly the same as the official readability measure. Both are manageable (see below).

"Lightness" that matches your eyes

The big difference is that OKLCH is a perceptual model. It was designed so that the numbers match what people actually see. It's based on a colour space called Oklab, published by Björn Ottosson in 2020,33 and it's now built into CSS, the language that styles websites, as oklch().34 Standard

The easiest way to see why this matters is to look. Below, the top row shows six colours that HSL says are all equally light. The grey strip under each one shows how light it really looks.

The three dials of OKLCH

You can think of OKLCH as three dials. Turn one and the other two stay put.

Lightness L 0 → 1

How light it looks, from black (0) to white (1). This is the dial that controls readability.

Chroma C 0 → ~0.37

How colourful it is. Zero is grey. The maximum depends on the hue and the lightness.

Hue H 0° → 360°

Which colour family, as an angle around a wheel. Every swatch in this row looks equally light.

Why OKLCH is so useful for a design system

Because the dials are independent and lightness matches your eyes, a lot of hard problems get easy. You can say "shade 700 of every colour is this light" and it will be true for blue, red and green alike. You can swap one brand colour for another by turning only the hue dial, without changing how light anything is, so readability doesn't break. Palettes become a recipe rather than a pile of hand-picked swatches. Gradients look cleaner. And OKLCH can describe the more vivid colours modern screens can show. It's supported in CSS and in the shared token format,3432 and Tailwind CSS, one of the most widely used styling frameworks, switched its whole default palette to OKLCH in version 4.0.35 Documented

Two things to watch out for

1. Some combinations can't be displayed. Screens can only show a certain range of colours. Very colourful shades that are also very light or very dark often fall outside that range. Good tools quietly turn down the chroma dial until the colour fits. Our palette generator does this and marks each colour where it happened.

2. OKLCH lightness isn't the official readability score. The accessibility guidelines measure contrast with a different formula.36 Equal OKLCH lightness gives similar readability across colours, not identical. You still check every pairing; 07.4 shows how close it gets.

07.3Building a palette, step by step

Step 1: start from your brand colour, but don't use it for everything

Most palettes start from a brand colour, and the first surprise is usually that the exact brand colour can't be used for text or for buttons with white text on them. Layer One's own orange, #ff6b3d, is a perfect example. On white it has a contrast ratio of just 2.83 to 1, well below the 4.5 to 1 the accessibility guidelines require for normal text. On the dark ink background, it reaches a comfortable 6.87 to 1. Standard

The fix isn't to change the brand. It's to treat the brand colour as a starting point for a family of shades, then use different shades for different jobs. The exact brand orange stays for big brand moments like the logo and illustrations. A deeper shade from the same family is used for buttons and links on light backgrounds. In the palette below, the brand family is generated from #ff6b3d, and shade 700 becomes the main action colour.

Step 2: add supporting colours for specific jobs

A product needs far fewer colours than a brand guideline suggests. Most products need one brand colour, a family of greys, and a few colours that signal status:

ColourIts jobRule of thumb
BrandMain actions, selected items, brand momentsNever reused to mean "error" or "success"
Neutral (greys)Text, backgrounds, borders: most of the screenVery slightly tinted, so it doesn't feel lifeless
RedErrors, destructive actions like "Delete"Clearly different from the brand colour
GreenSuccess, confirmationAlways paired with an icon or words
AmberWarnings, pending statesUse dark text on amber, not white
BlueLinks, information, keyboard focus outlinesCan double as the brand colour if your brand is blue

One important rule: colour should never be the only way to tell people something. Colour blindness is common, screens and lighting vary, and WCAG 2.2 requires that colour isn't the only visual signal.13 Standard So a red error message also gets an icon and clear words.

Watch for clashes between your brand and your status colours, too. Ledgerly's orange sits at hue 37° and its error red at 25°, only 12° apart. That's common with warm brands, and it means colour alone could never tell "main action" from "delete". The answer isn't a different colour. It's design: delete buttons get clear labels and a confirmation step, and errors always come with an icon.

Step 3: build each colour into a family of shades

New wordRampA family of shades of one colour, from very light to very dark, numbered like 50, 100, 200 … 950.

Each colour becomes a ramp: a set of shades numbered from very light (50) to very dark (950). The clever part, and the reason we use OKLCH, is that each shade number has the same lightness in every colour. Blue 700, red 700 and grey 700 are all equally light (L ≈ 0.485). So the number itself tells you something useful: "anything 700 or darker is safe for text on white".

Shade50100200300400500600700800900950
Lightness0.9750.9450.8850.8150.7300.6450.5650.4850.4050.3300.255
Colourfulness12%26%50%74%92%100%100%92%78%60%45%
Typical useBackgrounds, tintsSoft fills, bordersStrong borders, iconsText-safe accents, buttonsText, dark-mode surfaces

Notice that the shades are bunched up at both ends. That's on purpose. Interfaces need lots of very light tints (backgrounds, hover states, selected rows) and several very dark shades (text, dark-mode surfaces), but only a few mid-tones. Other well-known systems take a similar purpose-driven approach: Radix Colors uses 12 steps, each with a stated job from "app background" to "high-contrast text",37 and Google's Material Design generates families of tones from a key colour.31 Documented

Step 4: shape the colourfulness

Colourfulness should peak in the middle of the ramp and fade towards both ends. Very light shades that are very colourful look neon; very dark shades that are very colourful look muddy. That's the "colourfulness" row in the table above. Where a shade would be too colourful for screens to show, the generator turns the chroma dial down until it fits, keeping lightness the same so readability stays predictable.

07.4Making sure people can read it

New wordContrast ratioHow different two colours are in brightness, from 1:1 (identical) to 21:1 (black on white). Higher is easier to read.

Readability is measured with a contrast ratio: a number that compares how bright the text is with how bright the background is. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 set three thresholds you'll use all the time:3638 Standard

4.5:1The minimum for normal text. (7:1 for the stricter AAA level.)
3:1The minimum for large text: about 24px, or about 19px if bold.
3:1The minimum for the edges of buttons and inputs, focus outlines and meaningful icons.

Because every ramp uses the same lightness curve, contrast behaves almost identically across colours. The chart below proves it: six colours, six lines that nearly sit on top of each other.

This also gives designers pairing rules they can use without a contrast checker. Because lightness is fixed per shade, readability between two shades depends mostly on how many steps apart they are:

The light grey text trap

The most common readability mistake is "secondary" text, like captions, timestamps and helper text, set in a pale grey because it looks refined. It's the main reason so many websites fail contrast checks. Fix it once, at the source: Ledgerly's secondary text colour points to grey 700, which reaches 5.99:1 on the background. Nothing lighter is allowed for text, and because every component uses that one named colour, every screen passes.

What about APCA?

You may hear about APCA, a newer way of measuring contrast that takes text size and weight into account and has been explored for future versions of the guidelines.39 Radix Colors, for example, tunes its text shades with it.37 It's promising, but today the WCAG 2 ratio is the official requirement. Use WCAG 2 to pass, and APCA as extra guidance if you like.

07.5Naming colours by their job

A palette is a box of paints. A colour system is the set of labels that says what each paint is for. This is the single most important idea in this chapter, so let's take it slowly.

There are two kinds of name. The first kind describes the colour: "blue 600", "grey 950". The second kind describes the job: "link text", "page background", "error message". Components only ever use the second kind. The job names point to the colour names.

New wordSemantic tokenA colour named by its job ("text-secondary") rather than its appearance ("grey-700"). It points to a raw colour.

The design systems world has formal names for these levels. Colour names are called primitive tokens (the raw ingredients). Job names are called semantic tokens ("semantic" just means "about meaning"). Some systems add a third level of component tokens for settings specific to one component. Every mature public design system we know of separates raw values from their jobs, even if they use different words for it.4041423 Documented

Why bother with two names?

Dark mode becomes a switch

Dark mode just changes which paint each job points to. No component changes.

Fixes happen in one place

If error text needs to be darker, you change one pointer, not every red in the product.

Checks are simple

"Is secondary text readable?" is one check, not an audit of every grey ever used for text.

The palette stays tidy

People choose from a short list of jobs, not 66 swatches, so new random colours stop appearing.

Do you need the third level?

Component settings add another layer to name, document and maintain. Use them if you support several brands or white-labelled versions that need to restyle specific components, or if one component genuinely needs to differ from the normal rule. Otherwise, components can use job names directly. Many teams start with two levels and add the third only when they need it. Practice

Naming the jobs

Pick a simple naming pattern so that people can guess names they haven't seen. That's Rule #3 of how we work: name things so people can guess them. This pattern works for most products: what kind of thing, then its role, then (if needed) a variation and a state.

color.bg.surface                      // backgrounds: canvas, surface, subtle
color.text.secondary                   // text: primary, secondary, disabled, link
color.border.strong                    // borders: default, strong
color.action.primary.bg.hover         // interactive: role, part, state
color.feedback.danger.text            // status: danger, warning, success, info

07.6Colours that respond: hover, press and focus

Buttons, links and other interactive elements need to change colour when you hover over them, press them, or reach them with the keyboard. There are two common ways to handle this.

Approach A — step along the ramp

Move one shade darker

Hover goes one shade darker in light mode (brand 700 → 800) and one lighter in dark mode. Simple, easy to check for readability, and every state has a name.

DefaultHoverPressedFocus
Approach B — add a see-through layer

Lay a tint on top

A faint, see-through layer is placed over the button on hover or press. Material Design uses this approach. It works on any colour and needs fewer names.

Default+ hover layer+ press layer

Focus deserves special attention. When someone moves through a page with the keyboard (many people do, and some have to), the focus outline shows where they are. It must contrast at least 3:1 with what's around it.38 Give it its own named colour (Ledgerly uses blue 600, which reaches 4.28:1 on the background) rather than reusing the brand colour, which may not stand out against the button it surrounds.

Disabled elements are exempt from contrast rules, but they still need to be recognisable. And never rely on a greyed-out button alone to explain why something can't be done. Tell people why.

07.7Dark mode, brands and white-labelling

Here's the payoff for all the naming work. A theme is simply a complete list of which paint each job points to. Below is the same little interface, built from the same named jobs, shown with two different lists.

Dark mode isn't just "invert the colours"

  • Avoid pure black. A very dark grey (Ledgerly uses grey 950) is easier on the eyes and leaves room to show depth.
  • Show depth with lighter surfaces. Shadows barely show on dark backgrounds, so raised cards and menus get slightly lighter instead.
  • Lighten the accent colours. Ledgerly's main action colour moves from brand 700 to brand 400 in dark mode, with dark text on top (5.96:1).
  • Check everything again. A pairing that passes in light mode can fail in dark mode, and the other way round.

IBM's Carbon, for example, offers four themes (two light, two dark) from a single set of colour jobs.41 Documented

Several brands, or customers' brands

SituationWhat changesHow to set it up
Light and darkWhich paint each job points toTwo pointer lists over one palette
Several brands you ownThe brand paints, sometimes fonts and corner roundingA brand level that swaps the brand paints, then light and dark per brand
White-label for customersA few things the customer chooses, like one colour and a logoGenerate the customer's ramp from their colour; let them change only those inputs

Practice White-labelling safely

Let the customer pick one brand colour, then generate their ramp using your lightness curve, and point your jobs at it. Because lightness is fixed per shade, their "brand 700" ends up exactly as light as yours, so readability survives a colour choice you didn't make. Run the pairing checks automatically and fall back to a darker shade if a colour falls short (as green does at 600).

07.8Questions teams always ask about colour

How many colours should a design system have?

Few colour families, plenty of shades, and fewer named jobs than you'd expect.

Most products need one brand colour, one grey family and three or four status colours: five to seven ramps. At 11 shades each, that's 55 to 77 paints, but only 30 to 60 named jobs, and the jobs are what people actually choose from. Practice

How many shades should each ramp have?

Between 10 and 13 is the normal range.

Tailwind uses 11, Radix 12 and Material 13.353731 Documented Fewer than about 9 leaves gaps for hover states and dark mode. More than about 13 gives you shades nobody can tell apart.

Is there a maximum?

No official one. The practical limit is how many your team can tell apart and remember.

The warning sign isn't the size of the palette. It's having several job names that mean almost the same thing: "text-muted", "text-subtle", "text-secondary", "text-tertiary". If you can't explain the difference between two names in one sentence, merge them.

How do we stop new colours creeping in?

Components use job names only, and an automatic check flags any colour code typed directly into product code. New job names need a reason ("which job doesn't exist yet?") and the owner's approval. And recount the "different colours in our code" number from Chapter 03 every quarter. It should go down.

How should we do gradients?

Blend in OKLCH, and name the start and end colours.

Blending in the traditional way passes through a dull, greyish middle. Blending in OKLCH keeps the middle bright and even. Modern CSS lets you choose which way to blend.

blended the traditional way (sRGB): blue 600 → amber 400
blended in OKLCH: blue 600 → amber 400
What about see-through colours and overlays?

Fine for overlays and hover layers; never for text.

The dark, see-through layer behind a pop-up dialog is a good use of transparency. Transparent text isn't: its readability changes depending on whatever is behind it, so you can't check it once and trust it. Give text solid colours.

Colour checklist

  • Palette built in OKLCH from one lightness curve
  • Brand colour used as a starting point; buttons use a readable shade
  • 5–7 colour families, 10–13 shades each, same numbering everywhere
  • Colour codes generated by a tool, not hand-picked
  • A deliberately tinted (or deliberately neutral) grey family
  • Simple pairing rules shared with designers
  • Raw colours and job names kept separate; components use job names only
  • A naming pattern written down
  • Hover, press, focus and disabled colours for every interactive role
  • Light and dark mode as two pointer lists
  • Every pairing checked automatically
  • Status colours always paired with an icon or words

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Use OKLCH: its lightness matches what eyes see, so palettes become predictable.
  2. Build each colour into a ramp where each shade number has the same lightness in every colour.
  3. Check readability with the WCAG ratios: 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for large text and UI edges.
  4. Name colours by their job and let components use only job names. Dark mode and new brands then become a switch.

Chapter 08

08

Typography systems

Most of what people look at in your product is text: labels, numbers, headings, messages. A typography system isn't just picking a nice font. It's deciding a small set of text styles, each with a clear job, that stay readable on every screen.

Read this if

You're choosing a font, setting up text sizes, or your screens feel cluttered and it's hard to tell what's important.

What you'll leave with
  1. How to choose a font for a product (not a poster).
  2. A complete, named set of text styles you can adapt.
  3. How text should differ between dashboards, mobile apps, enterprise tools and more.

In this chapter

  1. 08.1Choosing a font
  2. 08.2Text sizes that work together
  3. 08.3Naming text by its job
  4. 08.4Text on different screen sizes
  5. 08.5Readable for everyone
  6. 08.6Different products need different type
  7. 08.7Turning text styles into tokens

08.1Choosing a font

When a brand team picks a font, they're usually thinking about a logo, a billboard or a headline. A product font has a harder job. It has to be readable at 12 pixels in a crowded table, show numbers that line up in columns, and work in every language you sell in. So for products, choosing a font is mostly a practical decision. Personality matters, but it comes second.

What to checkHow to check itWhy it matters
Readable when smallLook at 12–14px samples on a real laptop screen. Can you tell I, l and 1 apart? O and 0?Labels, tables and captions are all small.
Enough weightsAt least regular, medium and semibold, or a "variable" font with a weight range.Bold and regular are how you show what's important.
Numbers that line upCheck for "tabular figures": numbers that are all the same width.So columns of amounts align in tables and dashboards.
Your languagesEvery script you use now or might soon: accented Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, Devanagari…A fallback font for one market breaks consistency.
LicenceCan you use it on the web, in apps, across all your products? Open-source fonts make this easy.A licence problem can block a launch.
File sizeHow much it adds to page load.Fonts are often among the largest files a page loads first.

The "do nothing" option

Every operating system has a built-in interface font: San Francisco on Apple devices, Roboto on Android, Segoe UI on Windows. They're very readable, free, load instantly and feel familiar. For internal tools they're often the best choice. The trade-off is that your product looks less distinctive.

How many fonts?

One for the interface is usually enough. A second, like a monospaced font for codes and IDs or a display font for marketing, is common. A third is rarely needed. This book uses one font for everything, plus a monospaced font for values a computer would read.

Variable fonts: one file, every weight

New wordVariable fontA single font file that can produce any weight (and sometimes width) in a range, instead of separate files for each.

Traditionally, regular, medium and bold were separate font files. A variable font stores a whole range of weights in one file.43 For a design system that means fewer files to load and exact weights to choose from. Systems still name a small set of weights, so "any weight" doesn't turn into "every weight".

08.2Text sizes that work together

New wordType scaleThe short, fixed list of text sizes a product uses, like 12, 14, 16, 18, 22, 28 and 36 pixels.

If anyone can pick any text size, you end up with 13, 14, 14.5, 15 and 16 pixels all over the product, and nothing quite looks related. A type scale fixes this: a short list of sizes that everyone chooses from.

A classic way to create one is to start from a base size (usually 16 pixels, the browser's default) and multiply by the same number each step up. That number is called the ratio. A small ratio gives you lots of sizes close together; a large ratio jumps quickly to big headlines.

In practice, a pure mathematical scale is a starting point, not the answer. Apps need several sizes clustered between 12 and 20 pixels (labels, body text, small headings) and only a few large ones. So most mature systems start from a ratio, then adjust by hand and round to whole numbers. Google's Material Design 3, for example, uses a hand-tuned set of 15 named styles rather than a strict formula.44 Documented

Line spacing: tighter as text gets bigger

The space between lines (designers call it line-height or leading) should get proportionally tighter as text gets bigger. Body text reads comfortably at about 1.4 to 1.6 times its size. Big headlines look loose and disconnected above about 1.2. We also round every line-height to a multiple of 4 pixels, so text lines up neatly with everything else on the page (Chapter 09 explains why 4).

Text sizeLine spacing (× size)How Ledgerly's scale was calculated
Up to 14pxabout 1.45Multiply the size by the target, then round to the nearest multiple of 4px. Small text ends up a little looser and large text a little tighter, which is the direction you want. Headings use the tighter targets at every size, so an 18px heading gets 24px, not the 28px of 18px body text.
15–20pxabout 1.5
21–32pxabout 1.3
33–48pxabout 1.2
Over 48pxabout 1.1

Letter spacing

Fonts are spaced for reading sizes. Blown up to headline size, the gaps between letters start to look too wide, so big headings usually get slightly tighter letter spacing. Very small text and ALL-CAPS labels go the other way and get slightly looser spacing, which makes them easier to read.

08.3Naming text by its job

Just like colours, text styles should be named by what they're for, not by their size. "Heading large" survives a redesign; "28px" doesn't. Five families of text cover almost every product:

Display

Big numbers and headlines: a dashboard total, a welcome message.

Heading

Page and section titles: the structure of a screen.

Body

Paragraphs, descriptions, table cells, form values.

Label

Buttons, tabs, form labels, menu items. Slightly bolder.

Caption

Timestamps, helper text, small print.

Making things stand out takes more than size

A common mistake is trying to show importance with size alone. You end up with a dozen sizes and a page that still feels flat. Weight (bold or regular), colour (dark or grey), capital letters and space around text are just as effective, and they don't add new sizes.

✕ Size is doing all the work

Invoices
Overdue
3 invoices totalling ₹2,40,000
Last reminder sent 2 days ago

✓ Size, weight, colour and space together

Invoices
Overdue
3 invoices totalling ₹2,40,000
Last reminder sent 2 days ago

The version on the right uses fewer sizes but is much clearer, because each level differs from the next in two or more ways at once.

08.4Text on different screen sizes

A 36-pixel heading looks great on a laptop and takes up half the screen on a phone. There are two ways to handle this.

Stepped

Different sizes per screen size

"Heading XL" is 28px on phones and 36px on larger screens. Simple, predictable, and easy to show in design files.

Fluid

Sizes that grow smoothly

Text grows gradually between a minimum and a maximum as the screen widens, using a CSS feature called clamp(). Tools like Utopia popularised this.45

For the engineers reading, here's what a fluid heading looks like in code, with the maths spelled out:

/* Heading XL: 28px on a 360px-wide phone → 36px on a 1280px-wide laptop */
--type-heading-xl-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.554rem + 0.87vw, 2.25rem);

/* growth  = (36 − 28) ÷ (1280 − 360) = 0.0087 → 0.87vw
   start   = 28 − 0.0087 × 360       = 24.87px → 1.554rem */

A mistake we see often

Fluid text that ignores zoom

If text size is based only on screen width, it won't get bigger when someone zooms in, which can fail the accessibility requirement that text can be enlarged to 200%.13 Standard Always include a fixed part (the rem part above) in the formula, and only make headings fluid. Keep body text at a steady, readable size.

On phones and tablets, there's another layer. iPhone and Android both let people choose a larger text size for every app on their device. Apple's guidelines encourage apps to support this, which it calls Dynamic Type.46 A design system for mobile apps should connect each of its text styles to the platform's built-in, adjustable text styles rather than fixing sizes in place.

08.5Readable for everyone

Accessibility for text isn't a separate project. Most of it is decided by the type system. Here's what to build in from the start:

RequirementWhat it means for your text stylesSource
Enough contrast4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text. Each text style uses a colour that passes (see Chapter 07).Standard WCAG 1.4.336
Can be enlargedText can be zoomed to 200% without anything being cut off. Use flexible units and let boxes grow.Standard WCAG 1.4.4
Survives spacing changesSome readers apply their own, wider line and letter spacing. Layouts mustn't break when they do, so avoid boxes with a fixed height around text.Standard WCAG 1.4.1247
Works on narrow screensContent fits a 320-pixel-wide screen without scrolling sideways (tables and maps excepted).Standard WCAG 1.4.1048
Comfortable line lengthAim for about 45–75 characters per line in long text. Very long lines are tiring to read.Documented Bringhurst49
Not too smallAvoid body text below 14px in dense web apps or 16px on mobile web. Keep 11–12px for captions and labels.Practice

08.6Different products need different type

The same principles produce quite different results depending on what you're building. A trading dashboard and a meditation app shouldn't have the same text system. Here's how we'd tune typography for common kinds of product. Platform defaults are documented; the rest comes from practice.

ProductBody textRatioWhat matters mostWatch out for
SaaS web app14–16pxabout 1.2Clear headings to navigate by; comfortable forms; 10–14 styles in total.Big marketing-site headings leaking into the app.
Enterprise software14px (13px dense)1.125–1.2Fitting a lot on screen; easy scanning; long working sessions.Text too small for people with weaker eyesight; offer a roomier mode.
Mobile appsiOS: 17pt; Android: 16spPlatform's ownUse the platform's text styles; support users' larger-text settings.4644 DocumentedFixed-height rows that cut text off when users enlarge it.
Desktop apps13–15px1.125–1.2Fit in with the operating system; dense menus and panels.Mixing system and brand fonts inconsistently.
Websites that resize16px1.2 → 1.25–1.33Headings that grow with the screen; steady body text; comfortable line length.Headings that wrap to five lines on phones.
Data-heavy dashboards13–14pxabout 1.125Numbers that line up; a big-number style for key figures; a monospaced font for IDs.Everything the same size; use weight and colour to show importance.

IBM's Carbon formalises a similar idea with two sets of text styles: a "productive" set for dense, task-focused screens, and an "expressive" set for marketing and storytelling pages.50 Documented If your company has both a busy app and a marketing site, consider two sets rather than one compromise.

08.7Turning text styles into tokens

Text uses two levels of named values, just like colour. The first level names individual values: the font family, each weight, each size. The second level bundles them into complete styles named by job, like "heading large". The shared token format has a built-in "typography" type for exactly this kind of bundle.32 Here's what that looks like:

// individual values
"font": {
  "family": { "sans": { "$type": "fontFamily", "$value": ["Schibsted Grotesk", "system-ui", "sans-serif"] } },
  "weight": { "semibold": { "$type": "fontWeight", "$value": 600 } }
},
// a complete style, named by its job
"type": { "heading": { "lg": {
  "$type": "typography",
  "$value": {
    "fontFamily": "{font.family.sans}", "fontWeight": "{font.weight.semibold}",
    "fontSize": { "value": 28, "unit": "px" }, "lineHeight": 1.29,
    "letterSpacing": { "value": -0.01, "unit": "em" }
  } } } }

Typography checklist

  • One interface font (plus a monospaced one if needed), tested at small sizes
  • Numbers that line up in tables
  • 10–15 styles named by job, not size
  • Line spacing rounded to multiples of 4px
  • Letter spacing set for headings and labels
  • A plan for screen sizes: stepped or fluid (with zoom support)
  • Layouts survive 200% zoom and readers' own spacing
  • Long text kept to about 45–75 characters per line
  • Mobile styles connected to users' text-size settings
  • The same named styles in Figma and in code

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Choose a product font for readability at small sizes, aligned numbers and language support first.
  2. Use a short, fixed list of sizes, with line spacing that gets tighter as text gets bigger.
  3. Name text styles by their job, and show importance with weight, colour and space as well as size.
  4. Build accessibility into the styles themselves: contrast, zoom and flexible boxes.

Chapter 09

09

Spacing systems

Spacing is the foundation people notice least and feel most. It's what makes a screen feel calm or cluttered, organised or confusing. And because everyone decides it "by eye", it's usually the first thing to drift.

Read this if

Your screens feel slightly "off" but nobody can say why, design reviews keep turning into debates about padding, or you need both a compact and a roomy layout.

What you'll leave with
  1. A base unit and a short list of spacing values, and why they work.
  2. A simple way to think about space inside and between things.
  3. How to offer compact and comfortable versions of the same screen.

In this chapter

  1. 09.1Why spacing matters so much
  2. 09.2Picking a base unit
  3. 09.3The spacing scale
  4. 09.4Space inside things, space between things
  5. 09.5Compact and comfortable
  6. 09.6Spacing on different screens, and common mistakes

09.1Why spacing matters so much

Space does three jobs on a screen. It groups things: we automatically read items that sit close together as belonging together. It shows importance: things with more room around them feel more important. And it creates rhythm: a repeating beat that makes a page feel calm and intentional.

When spacing is chosen screen by screen, each value can be defended on its own, but together they're noise: 13 pixels here, 14 there, 22 somewhere else. People using the product don't notice the numbers. They notice that it feels a bit untidy, and they trust it a little less. Look at the same form below, spaced two ways.

09.2Picking a base unit

A spacing system starts with one small number, the base unit, and every spacing value is a multiple of it. Think of it like the smallest Lego stud: everything you build is a whole number of studs. The two common choices are 8 pixels and 4 pixels.

8px base

Fewer, clearer choices

Easy to think about, and most screen sizes divide neatly by 8. Atlassian's design system, for example, builds its spacing on an 8px base, with a few smaller steps for tight spots.51 Documented

4px base

Finer control for busy screens

Lets you use 12, 20 and 28, which matter for small components, icons and line spacing. Google's Material uses a 4dp grid for text and icons alongside an 8dp grid for layout.52 Documented

Practice Our recommendation

Use a 4px base with an 8px rhythm. Every value is a multiple of 4, and most of the values people actually reach for are multiples of 8. You get the precision small components need without the endless choice of "any number will do". Set line spacing for text (Chapter 08) to the same 4px grid, so text and boxes share one rhythm.

09.3The spacing scale

The scale is the fixed list of spacing values people can choose from. It should have lots of options at the small end, where 4 pixels is a visible difference, and only a few at the large end, where nobody can tell 64 from 68.

Naming spacing values

Different systems name spacing in different ways. Any of them works, as long as you pick one and stick to it:

StyleExampleGoodNot so good
Count of base unitsspace-6 = 24pxEasy to guess; easy mathsChanging the base unit renames everything
Multiplier × 100space.300 = 3 × 8px (Atlassian)51Room for in-between stepsLess obvious at a glance
Numbered stepsspacing-06 = 24px (IBM Carbon)30Short; stable orderYou have to look up every value
T-shirt sizesspace-mdFriendlyRuns out of names (xxxl?); hard to add a size in between

Our advice: choose the style your engineers can read without a lookup table.

09.4Space inside things, space between things

It helps to think about three kinds of space. Nathan Curtis gave them simple names that have stuck: inset (padding inside a box), stack (space between things stacked vertically) and inline (space between things side by side).53 Naming the kind of space, not just the amount, makes design specs and code reviews much clearer.

A useful rule of thumb is to use smaller values inside things and larger values between bigger groups:

Where the space isTypical valuesExamples
Inside a component4–16pxGap between an icon and its label; padding inside a button or input
Between related items8–16pxA label and its field; one field and the next; list items
Between groups24–32pxSections of a form; gaps between cards
Between page sections40–64pxMajor sections of a page
Page edges16–80pxGrows with screen size (see Chapter 10)

The golden rule: space within a group must always be clearly smaller than space between groups. A handy way to guarantee it is to jump at least two steps on the scale between levels: 8 → 16 → 24 or 32. That keeps relationships obvious, even when different designers make their own sensible choices. Practice

09.5Compact and comfortable

Think about two very different people using the same invoices table. An accountant at month-end wants to see 200 rows without scrolling. A small business owner checking one invoice on a Sunday wants things roomy and easy to tap. Density is how much fits in a given space, and good systems let you offer both, by switching a few spacing values rather than building separate components.

There's a floor to how compact you can go, set by people's fingers and by accessibility rules. WCAG 2.2 requires click and tap targets of at least 24 by 24 pixels, with some exceptions.54 Standard For touchscreens, platform guidelines go further: Apple recommends at least 44 by 44 points,55 and Google's Material recommends 48 by 48.52 Documented So compact modes are for mouse-and-keyboard use on desktop. Don't make them the default on phones.

SettingCompactDefaultComfortable
Height of buttons and inputs32px40px48px
Padding inside buttons and inputs8px12px16px
Padding inside table rows4px8px12px
Space between form fields12px16px24px

09.6Spacing on different screens, and common mistakes

Here's a simple principle. Spacing inside components shouldn't change with screen size: a button has the same padding on a phone and a laptop. Spacing in the layout should: the margins around the page and the gaps between sections grow when there's more room. You can build that split into your named values. For engineers, it looks like this:

/* The scale itself never changes */
--space-2: 8px;  --space-4: 16px;  --space-6: 24px;  --space-10: 40px;  --space-16: 64px;

/* Layout spacing grows on bigger screens */
--space-page-margin:  var(--space-4);     /* 16px on phones          */
--space-section-gap:  var(--space-10);
@media (min-width: 840px) {
  --space-page-margin: var(--space-6);   /* 24px on larger screens  */
  --space-section-gap: var(--space-16);
}

/* Component spacing changes with density, not screen size */
--space-control-inset-x: var(--space-3);

Four mistakes we see again and again

Mistake

"Just this once" values

Each one seems harmless. Fifty of them add up to a second, invisible spacing system. Set up an automatic check for spacing values that aren't on the scale.

Mistake

The same spacing everywhere

Using 16px for everything removes the grouping signal, and groups disappear. Vary space on purpose.

Mistake

Components with built-in outside margins

A component that adds its own space around itself collides unpredictably with others. Let the container decide the gaps between its contents.

Mistake

Forgetting about line spacing

A 16px gap between two blocks of loosely spaced text looks bigger than 16px. Keep text on the same 4px rhythm so measured and visible space match.

Spacing checklist

  • A base unit chosen (we recommend 4px with an 8px rhythm)
  • A fixed list of about 12–14 values
  • Names that tell you the size
  • Inset, stack and inline used in specs
  • Space within groups clearly smaller than space between them
  • Compact and comfortable modes; touch targets big enough
  • Component spacing fixed; layout spacing grows with screen size
  • An automatic check for off-scale values

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Space groups things, shows importance and sets rhythm. It's never just "empty".
  2. Pick a base unit (4px is our recommendation) and a short, fixed list of values.
  3. Keep space inside groups clearly smaller than space between them.
  4. Offer density modes by changing a few values, and respect minimum tap sizes on touchscreens.

Up next →Chapter 10: Grid and layout systems

Chapter 10

10

Grid and layout systems

A layout system decides where things go on every screen size before anyone designs a single page. Done well, nobody notices it. Done badly, every screen breaks in its own special way on someone's phone.

Read this if

You're deciding how your product adapts to different screens, designing a dashboard, or your pages look fine on your laptop and fall apart elsewhere.

What you'll leave with
  1. The parts of a layout grid, in plain language, with real numbers.
  2. How to choose the screen widths where your layout changes.
  3. A practical way to lay out dashboards and complex business software.

In this chapter

  1. 10.1What a grid is
  2. 10.2Where the layout changes: breakpoints
  3. 10.3Stretchy, fixed, or both
  4. 10.4Laying out a dashboard
  5. 10.5Phones, desktops and what lines up with what
  6. 10.6Layouts for complex business software

10.1What a grid is

Look at a newspaper. The text sits in columns, photos span one, two or three of them, and everything lines up even though dozens of people worked on the page. That's a grid at work. On screens, grids do the same job: they make things line up without anyone measuring.

A layout grid splits the width of the screen into columns, with fixed gaps between them called gutters. Around the outside there are margins, and the whole thing sits inside a container. Content spans whole columns (plus the gutters between them), so edges line up across the page.

PartWhat it isRule of thumb
ColumnsThe vertical strips content lines up to.4 on phones, 8 on tablets, 12 on laptops and desktops.
GuttersThe fixed gaps between columns.Use a value from the spacing scale (16–24px). Gutters stay fixed; columns stretch.
MarginsThe space between the grid and the edge of the screen.Grows with screen size: 16px on phones, up to 32–80px on big screens.
ContainerThe box the grid lives in, sometimes with a maximum width.Cap the width of reading pages (around 1200–1440px); let busy apps use the full width.

10.2Where the layout changes: breakpoints

New wordBreakpointA screen width at which the layout changes, for example from one column to two.

A breakpoint is a screen width where your layout rearranges itself: the side menu tucks away, two columns become one, and so on. The trick is to set breakpoints where your layout needs to change, guided by common types of device, rather than chasing specific phone models, which change every year. Here's how two of the most mature design systems do it:

Google Material 3 Documented

Size classWidth
Compact (phones)< 600
Medium (small tablets)600–839
Expanded (tablets, small laptops)840–1199
Large1200–1599
Extra-large≥ 1600

Source: Material 3 layout guidance.56

IBM Carbon Documented

NameFrom (px)Columns
sm3204
md6728
lg105616
xlg131216
max158416

Source: Carbon 2x Grid.57 Its 16 columns suit dense business screens.

Two respected systems, two different sets of numbers, and both work well. The lesson isn't to copy either. Pick four or five breakpoints, give them names rather than device names ("medium", not "iPad"), and share them as named values so design and code agree. Ledgerly uses Material's size classes with 4, 8 and 12 columns.

10.3Stretchy, fixed, or both

Fluid

Stretches to fill the screen

Uses all the space. Great for busy apps, but lines of text get uncomfortably long on wide screens.

Fixed

Always the same width

Predictable and easy to design, but wastes space on big screens and needs separate layouts for small ones.

Both (recommended)

Stretches, up to a limit

Columns stretch with the screen until a maximum width. Reading pages use the limit; busy apps can skip it.

How wide should content be?

The grid decides where things can go. Separately, you should decide how wide some things should be. Paragraphs are easiest to read at around 45–75 characters per line,49 so body text should rarely stretch across all 12 columns of a big screen. Forms work best narrow, too. Set these widths as their own named values:

Named widthValueUsed for
width-prose68 charactersArticles, help pages, long descriptions
width-form560pxSingle-column forms and settings
width-dialog560pxStandard pop-up dialogs
width-page1440pxMaximum width for reading and marketing pages
width-appnoneBusy app screens that use the full width

10.4Laying out a dashboard

Most business software isn't really a set of pages on a grid. It's a frame (a top bar and a side menu that stay put) around a content area that changes. If the design system defines the frame once, every team stops reinventing it, and every product feels like part of the same family.

Four dashboard rules that always help

  1. Most important thing at the top left

    In left-to-right languages, people start reading at the top left. Put the number that answers "is everything OK?" there.

  2. Cards in a row share a height

    Matching heights keep the grid visible and make side-by-side comparison easy.

  3. A short list of widths

    Allow cards to span 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 or 12 columns. Avoid 5 and 7, which create edges that don't line up with anything.

  4. Flip for right-to-left languages

    Build with "start" and "end" rather than "left" and "right", so Arabic and Hebrew layouts mirror correctly from the same design.

10.5Phones, desktops and what lines up with what

A phone layout isn't a shrunken desktop

On a phone, the side menu becomes a bottom bar or a slide-out drawer, side-by-side panels become separate screens with a back button, and wide tables become lists or cards. Decide these changes once, as patterns, and every product gets them for free.

Big things line up to columns; small things line up to each other

Page sections and cards line up to grid columns. Inside a card, elements line up with each other using spacing values. A button doesn't need to snap to a column. Trying to grid everything makes components rigid and awkward.

The narrow-screen rule

WCAG 2.2 requires content to fit a screen 320 pixels wide without scrolling sideways, except for things that genuinely need two dimensions, like data tables, maps and diagrams.48 Standard Plan the 320px version of every pattern. Only ever scroll sideways inside a table, never the whole page.

10.6Layouts for complex business software

Big enterprise tools push past a simple page grid. Think of an email app with a folder list, a message list and a reading pane side by side, or a CRM where you resize panels to fit your work. Your layout system needs words and rules for these too:

Several panes side by side

List and detail views that sit side by side on big screens and become separate screens on small ones. Material documents these as standard layouts.56

Panels you can resize or fold

People who use a tool all day expect to resize panels. Set minimum and maximum widths as named values, and remember each person's choice.

Components that fit their space

A component in a narrow side panel should adapt to its panel, not the whole screen. A newer CSS feature called container queries makes this possible.

Headers that stay put

Table headers that stay visible while scrolling, first columns that stay fixed, and sideways scrolling inside tables keep people oriented in large data sets.

Layout values, written down

Like everything else, layout decisions become named values that design and code share:

"breakpoint": { "medium": "600px", "expanded": "840px", "large": "1200px", "xlarge": "1600px" },
"grid":       { "columns": { "compact": 4, "medium": 8, "expanded": 12 },
                "gutter": "{space.4}", "margin": { "compact": "{space.4}", "expanded": "{space.6}" } },
"layout":     { "sidebar": { "width": "240px", "folded": "64px" }, "topbar": { "height": "48px" },
                "width": { "prose": "68ch", "form": "560px", "page": "1440px" } }

A note for engineers: CSS variables can't be used inside media query conditions, so breakpoint values are turned into fixed constants (in Sass or JavaScript, for example) rather than CSS variables.

Layout checklist

  • 4–5 named breakpoints, shared by design and code
  • Columns for each (for example 4 / 8 / 12)
  • Gutters and margins taken from the spacing scale
  • Stretchy layouts with a maximum width for reading pages
  • Named widths for text, forms and dialogs
  • The app frame (top bar, side menu) defined once
  • Phone versions of each pattern decided once
  • Everything works at 320px wide (tables excepted)
  • "Start" and "end" instead of "left" and "right"
  • Components that adapt to the panel they're in

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. A grid is columns, gutters, margins and a container. It makes things line up without measuring.
  2. Choose a few named breakpoints where your layout genuinely needs to change.
  3. Stretch layouts to a limit, and cap the width of text and forms for readability.
  4. Define the app frame and the phone versions of patterns once, so every team inherits them.

Chapter 11

11

How foundations work together

Colour, type, spacing and layout aren't four separate projects. They're one system. The easiest way to see that is to follow a single button from the first decision all the way to the code that ships.

Read this if

You want to see the whole picture in one place, or you need to explain to engineers how design foundations become working components.

What you'll leave with
  1. One button, traced through every layer from decision to code.
  2. What changes, and what doesn't, when a foundation changes.
  3. A checklist to confirm your foundations are ready before you build components.

In this chapter

  1. 11.1One button, five layers
  2. 11.2Into the code
  3. 11.3What happens when something changes
  4. 11.4Are your foundations ready?

11.1One button, five layers

The main "primary" button is the most-used interactive element in most products, which makes it the perfect example. Here's every foundation it depends on, and how each one travels from a decision to the screen.

The button, labelled

11.2Into the code

This section is mostly for engineers, but it's worth a look even if you don't write code, because it shows the payoff. An automatic build step turns the list of named values into whatever each platform needs. For websites, that's CSS variables. The button's own code then uses only those names. Look closely: there isn't a single colour code or pixel value typed into the button itself.

/* tokens.css: generated automatically, never edited by hand */
:root {
  --color-brand-700: oklch(0.486 0.172 35);
  --color-brand-800: oklch(0.406 0.146 34);
  --color-action-primary-bg:
    var(--color-brand-700);
  --color-action-primary-bg-hover:
    var(--color-brand-800);
  --space-control-inset-x: var(--space-4);
  --size-control-height: 40px;
}
/* dark mode: only the pointers change */
[data-theme="dark"] {
  --color-action-primary-bg:
    var(--color-brand-400);
}
/* compact mode: only the sizes change */
[data-density="compact"] {
  --size-control-height: 32px;
  --space-control-inset-x: var(--space-2);
}
/* button.css: uses names only */
.button {
  height: var(--size-control-height);
  padding-inline: var(--space-control-inset-x);
  gap: var(--space-2);
  border-radius: var(--radius-control);
  font: var(--type-label-md);
}
.button[data-variant="primary"] {
  background: var(--color-action-primary-bg);
  color: var(--color-action-primary-text);
}
.button[data-variant="primary"]:hover {
  background:
    var(--color-action-primary-bg-hover);
}
.button:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--color-focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

iPhone and Android apps get the same values, generated from the same source file into their own languages. The source file is the agreement; each platform's components are just different ways of honouring it.

11.3What happens when something changes

The real test of all this work is change. Here's what each common change touches, and, just as importantly, what it doesn't.

The changePaintsJobsComponentsProductsThe work involved
Rebrand with a new colour●○○○Change one starting colour; shades regenerate; check readability; release.
Add dark mode○●○○One new list of pointers; check every pairing; release.
Make secondary text more readable○●○○Change one pointer; every product is fixed when it updates.
Add a compact mode○●◐○New spacing values; check components with fixed internal sizes.
New set of text sizes●◐○◐Values change; products check any layouts that relied on old sizes.
White-label for a customer●○○○Generate a brand family from the customer's colour.

● changes · ◐ worth checking · ○ untouched. These results only hold if components use named values everywhere. A single colour code typed directly into a component breaks the chain for that component.

Part 02 in one sentence

Decide once, name everything, and let components use only the names. Then almost every future change becomes a settings change instead of a rebuild.

11.4Are your foundations ready?

Before you start building components at scale, run through this list. Each item points back to the chapter that explains it.

Colour ch. 07

  • Shade families built in OKLCH, with colour codes generated by a tool
  • Job names for backgrounds, text, borders, icons, actions, status and focus
  • Light and dark lists, with every pairing checked automatically

Typography ch. 08

  • Text styles named by job, saved as bundles
  • Line spacing on the 4px grid; numbers that line up
  • A plan for screen sizes that respects zoom

Spacing ch. 09

  • A 4px-based scale with names that tell you the size
  • Component spacing with compact and comfortable modes
  • Tap targets big enough for fingers

Layout ch. 10

  • Named breakpoints, columns, gutters and margins
  • The app frame and content widths defined
  • Every pattern planned for a 320px screen

Plumbing ch. 06

  • One source file of named values, turned automatically into code and Figma
  • An automatic check against colour codes typed into product code

Tokens first, components second.Rule #4 — Layer One

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Every visual detail of a component should come from a named value.
  2. Each layer only knows about the one below it, and that's what makes change safe.
  3. Rebrands, dark mode and readability fixes become changes to names, not to components.
  4. With foundations in place, you're ready for components, which is where Part 03 begins.

03

Components: designing, building and looking after them

Components are the part of a design system people actually touch every day: the buttons, fields, menus and tables everyone builds with. This part covers how to decide which ones to build, how to design and build them so they last, and how to keep a growing library easy to find, trust and use.

  1. 12Components, explained
  2. 13Deciding what to build first
  3. 14Designing a component that lasts
  4. 15Building components in code
  5. 16A library people can actually use

Chapter 12

12

Components, explained

Buttons, text fields, menus, tables: components are what most people picture when they hear "design system". This chapter takes one apart, piece by piece, so you understand what you're actually building before you build a single one.

Read this if

You're new to components, you're about to plan a component library, or you've heard words like "variant", "prop" and "slot" and want them explained simply.

What you'll leave with
  1. What a component really is, in design and in code.
  2. The vocabulary: parts, options, states and slots.
  3. A realistic sense of how many components a product needs.

In this chapter

  1. 12.1What a component is
  2. 12.2Anatomy: the parts of a component
  3. 12.3Options: types, sizes and settings
  4. 12.4States: one component, many situations
  5. 12.5Small parts and big parts
  6. 12.6How many components do you need?

12.1What a component is

Think about the light switches in your home. You don't design a new switch for every room. You pick one model, and every room gets the same one. It works the same way everywhere, you know exactly what it does, and if a better model comes out, you can swap them all.

A component is the same idea for software: a piece of interface that's designed once, built once and used everywhere. A button. A text field. A dropdown menu. A date picker. A table.

The important part, and the part people often miss, is that a design system component exists twice, as a pair of twins. One twin lives in the design tool, where designers drag it into their screens. The other lives in code, where engineers use it to build the real product. The two twins have the same name, the same options and the same behaviour. When the twins match, a designer's screen and the shipped product match too.

The design twin

In Figma (or similar)

A "master" that designers place into screens. Change the master and every copy in every design file can update.

The code twin

In the code package

A piece of code engineers use with one line, like <Button variant="primary">Save</Button>. Improve it and every screen gets the improvement on the next update.

ScenarioWhen the twins don't match
The situation

The Figma button has four types: primary, secondary, tertiary and danger. The code button has three, and calls them "solid", "outline" and "ghost".

What goes wrong

A designer uses "tertiary" in a design. The engineer guesses it means "ghost". It doesn't quite match. Design review flags it. Everyone loses half a day.

The fix

One list of names and options, agreed once and used in both places. Chapter 15 covers how to keep the twins in step.

12.2Anatomy: the parts of a component

Even a simple component is made of several parts, and naming them makes design discussions much faster. "The helper text is too close to the field" is a lot clearer than "that grey bit underneath is a bit squashed". Here's an ordinary text field, taken apart.

Every component in your system should have an anatomy diagram like this in its documentation. It gives designers, engineers and writers a shared map, and it's where many accessibility decisions get made. In the example, the label is always visible, even while typing, because placeholder text that disappears as you type is a common usability and accessibility problem.

12.3Options: types, sizes and settings

New wordVariantAn approved version of a component, like a primary or a secondary button. Same component, different look for a different purpose.

A single component usually comes in a few approved versions. A button might come in a primary version for the main action on a screen, a secondary version for less important actions, and a danger version for things like "Delete account". It might also come in three sizes. Designers call these variants; engineers often call the settings that control them props (short for "properties"). They're the same idea: the switches and dials on a component.

Options are powerful, but they're also where components go wrong. Every option you add is something to design, build, test, document and maintain, for every combination. Three types and three sizes is nine combinations. Add "with icon" and "loading" and it's thirty-six. That's why mature systems are careful about adding options. A good question to ask before adding one: is this a real, repeated need in more than one team, or a one-off for a single screen?

A mistake we see often

The button with forty settings

Every team asks for one small option: a different colour, a different corner, a special icon position. Each request is reasonable, and the system team says yes each time. Two years later the button has forty settings, nobody understands them all, and it's slower to use the system button than to build your own. Saying "no" (or "build that locally") is part of looking after a component.

12.4States: one component, many situations

A component doesn't just sit there looking nice. People hover over it, click it, tab to it with the keyboard, type into it, make mistakes in it. Each of these situations is called a state, and each one needs to be designed. Here's a text field in eight of them.

When a component looks broken in production, it's very often because a state was never designed. Nobody thought about what happens when the text is too long, or when the data is still loading, or when there's an error and the field is also disabled. Designing every state up front is one of the biggest quality gains a design system gives you. Chapter 14 includes a full checklist.

12.5Small parts and big parts

Some components are small and simple: a button, a checkbox, a badge. Others are made from several smaller ones: a search bar is a text field, an icon and a button; a data table is made of headers, cells, checkboxes and pagination. Brad Frost's Atomic Design popularised this idea of building big things from small things, a bit like atoms making molecules.2

New wordSlotAn empty space inside a component where you can put other content, like a picture frame you fill yourself.

For bigger components, there's an important design choice. Do you give the component lots of settings to cover every case, or do you give it slots, empty spaces where teams can put their own content? A card is a good example. Instead of building "card with image", "card with avatar", "card with chart" and so on, you build one card with a few slots and let teams fill them.

Slots aren't always the answer. A button shouldn't have a slot for "anything you like", because then someone puts a dropdown inside it. As a rough rule: small, frequently used components should be strict, with a few clear options; larger, container-like components should be flexible, with slots. Alla Kholmatova's book Design Systems describes this as a balance between strict and loose systems, and points out that more modular isn't automatically better.58

12.6How many components do you need?

Fewer than you'd think, at least to start. Most products are built from a surprisingly small set of everyday components. The table below is a typical starting set for a business web app. It's not a rule, but if you're planning your first year, it's a realistic shape. Practice

GroupComponentsCount
ActionsButton, icon button, link3
Form inputsText field, text area, select, checkbox, radio, switch, date picker, search8
FeedbackAlert / banner, toast, inline message, progress, spinner, empty state6
ContainersCard, dialog, side panel, accordion, tabs5
NavigationTop bar, side menu, breadcrumbs, pagination, menu5
Data displayTable, badge, tag, avatar, tooltip5
Total32

Systems grow over time, of course. At IBM, Layer One's founder worked on systems with 71 components for an airline and more than 40 for a pharmacy storefront.1 But even those started with the everyday basics. The order you build them in matters a lot, and that's the subject of the next chapter.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. A component is designed once, built once and used everywhere, and it exists as twins in design and code with identical names and options.
  2. Name a component's parts (its anatomy) so everyone can talk about it precisely.
  3. Options multiply effort; add them only for real, repeated needs.
  4. Design every state, not just the default. Use slots for big, container-like components.
